newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO ministers to meet on new Bosnia force.
newsitem.headline: NATO ministers to meet on new Bosnia force.

text.p: NATO defence ministers meet in Norway this week for their first formal discussions of what follow-on force to keep in Bosnia after the current mission's mandate ends in late-December.
Western allies accept that a force will have to stay to prevent conflict and give the Dayton peace accords time to take root, but its size, make-up and mandate have yet to be agreed.
The issue is highly sensitive in the United States where presidential elections take place on November 5.

President Bill Clinton originally promised that U.S. troops would be in Bosnia no longer than the current mandate for the 55,000-strong force. But America's main European allies have made clear they will not stay without a U.S. troop commitment.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said last week the alliance would have to remain engaged beyond the end of the year, probably with a smaller force including U.S. troops.
"I believe that the international community, including NATO, must remain engaged in Bosnia beyond this first year," he said in a speech to the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London.
His was the latest voice in a chorus that argues the peace process in Bosnia will need foreign nursing for at least a year or two more.

Carl Bildt, the international community's representative in Bosnia who is charged with overseeing the civilian aspects of Dayton, says the benefits of a year of peace will be lost if a strong deterrent force does not remain.

Countrywide elections just over a week ago underlined Bosnia's ethnic divide and highlighted the difficult problems ahead in trying to create the common institutions foreseen in Dayton to reunify the country.

Even with NATO mounting a big security operation, few refugees took the risk of crossing ethnic boundaries to vote in their former homes. "It shows how quickly things could deteriorate if NATO was not there," said one NATO official.
The timetable for withdrawal of the NATO-led implementation force has already slipped.
NATO has promised they will be no significant withdrawal of its force before municipal elections take place.

They were cancelled by international poll organisers because of irregularities in the registration of voters, but potentially could be far more difficult to police as thousands are expected to return to vote for local administrations.
"The municipals are really important, and a security nightmare... Moslems want to get pockets in Serb territory and the Serbs want them to legitimise their control," said one independent analyst.
The two-day meeting in the Norwegian town of Bergen will be briefed on the likely new date for those polls.

Robert Frowick, head of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission in Bosnia, has been under pressure to call those polls for November, but independent analysts say they should be put off until next spring.
Many countries, however, also want to demonstrate that a "new NATO", capable of future Bosnia-style missions, is beginning to take shape.
Germany has already indicated it may commit ground troops and a more flexible, less U.S.-dominated command structure, with Russian participation, could be given a first run-out.
Former Warsaw Pact states, such as Poland and Hungary, want to build up the links they forged by taking part in the first mission.

They want to remain and see close cooperation in the new force as a way of strenthening their case for full NATO membership early next year -- an issue which will require a new NATO-Russia deal on European security.
Last Wednesday, NATO agreed to set up a new headquarters in Bosnia, ostensibly to oversee the year-end withdrawal. But it could also serve to coordinated a smaller replacement force.
